title: Ἀνθρακεὺς καὶ γναφεύς
part: The Charcoal-Burner and the Fuller (Chambry 56 · Perry 29)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 56 (= Perry 29). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνθρακεὺς ἐπί τινος οἰκίας ἐργαζόμενος, ὡς ἐθεάσατο γναφέα αὐτῷ παροικισθέντα, προσελθὼν παρεκάλει αὐτόν, ὅπως αὐτῷ σύνοικος γένηται, διεξιὼν ὡς οἰκειότεροι ἀλλήλοις ἔσονται καὶ λυσιτελέστερον διάξουσι μίαν ἔπαυλιν οἰκοῦντες.
sentences.tr: Anthrakeus epi tinos oikias ergazomenos, hōs etheasato gnaphea autōi paroikisthenta, proselthōn parekalei auton, hopōs autōi synoikos genētai, diexiōn hōs oikeioteroi allēlois esontai kai lysitelesteron diaxousi mian epaulin oikountes.
sentences.l: A charcoal-burner working in a certain house, when he saw a fuller settled next door to him, having-come-up urged him to become his housemate, setting-out that they would be more intimate with one another and would live more profitably inhabiting a single dwelling.
sentences.i: A charcoal-burner who was working in a certain house, when he saw that a fuller had settled next door, went up and urged him to share the house with him, explaining that they would be closer to one another and would live more profitably under one roof.
sentences.n: An ἀνθρακεύς burns wood down into charcoal — filthy, sooty work; a γναφεύς cleans and whitens cloth. The two trades are opposites, and that is the whole fable. ὅπως with the subjunctive after παρεκάλει gives the content of the request, 'urged him that he should become'; διεξιὼν ὡς… is 'explaining that…', ὡς after a verb of saying, interchangeable here with ὅτι.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ γναφεὺς ὑποτυχὼν ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔμοιγε τοῦτο παντελῶς ἀδύνατον· ἃ γὰρ ἐγὼ λευκανῶ, σὺ ασβολώσεις. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho gnapheus hypotychōn ephē· « All’ emoige touto pantelōs adynaton· ha gar egō leukanō, sy asbolōseis. »
sentences.l: And the fuller, taking-him-up, said: « But for me at least this is wholly impossible; for what I shall whiten, you will blacken with soot. »
sentences.i: And the fuller answered: « But for me that is quite impossible: whatever I whiten, you will smudge with soot. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών, literally 'having taken up (the word)', is the standing fable idiom for 'answered'. Each man reaches for his own trade-word: λευκανῶ is the future of λευκαίνω, to whiten, the fuller's business; ἀσβολώσεις is from ἄσβολος, soot. ἔμοιγε is ἐμοί with the emphasizing γε, 'for me at any rate'; ἐστι is left unexpressed with ἀδύνατον.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι πᾶν τὸ ἀνόμοιον ἀκοινώνητόν ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti pan to anomoion akoinōnēton esti.
sentences.l: The story shows that everything unlike is incapable of partnership.
sentences.n: πᾶν τὸ ἀνόμοιον is the neuter article with an adjective, 'everything that is unlike'. ἀκοινώνητον is built from κοινωνέω, to have a share in common — 'not to be shared in'.
